questions.q: What does setting Object Ownership to 'ACLs disabled (Bucket owner enforced)' do?
options: Every object is owned by the bucket's account, and access runs only through policies, never legacy per-object ACLs
It permanently deletes all objects currently owned by other accounts
It enables public access to every object in the bucket
It disables bucket policies and requires ACLs instead
questions.explain: Bucket owner enforced is AWS's recommended default: ownership is centralized and access is controlled entirely by policies, not legacy ACLs.

questions.q: A bucket has Block Public Access turned OFF at the bucket level, but the AWS account has it fully ON at the account level. What happens?
options: The bucket remains protected — S3 enforces the most restrictive combination of account- and bucket-level settings
The bucket becomes publicly accessible because bucket-level settings always win
S3 throws an error and refuses to serve any requests to the bucket
Account-level Block Public Access only applies to newly created buckets, not existing ones
questions.explain: S3 always applies the most restrictive combination of bucket-level and account-level Block Public Access settings — the account-wide block still wins.

questions.q: What is a bucket policy, technically?
options: A resource-based IAM policy, written as JSON, attached directly to the bucket
A client-side configuration file stored only in the AWS CLI
The same thing as an ACL, just renamed
A policy that can only be created through AWS Organizations, never per-bucket
questions.explain: A bucket policy is a resource-based JSON IAM policy attached directly to the S3 bucket, distinct from identity-based IAM policies and from legacy ACLs.

questions.q: In the lesson's example bucket policy, what does the 'DenyInsecureTransport' statement do?
options: Explicitly denies any S3 request not made over TLS, for every principal including the bucket owner
Allows any request as long as it uses HTTP instead of HTTPS
Only applies to the specific IAM role named in the first statement
Grants public read access to the bucket over HTTPS only
questions.explain: The condition checks aws:SecureTransport == false and applies Deny to Principal '*', meaning it blocks non-TLS requests for everyone, overriding any Allow elsewhere.

questions.q: Why does Block Public Access exist as a separate layer from bucket policies at all?
options: It acts as an override safety switch that refuses to honor public grants from a policy or ACL, without needing to edit that policy itself
It replaces bucket policies entirely once enabled
It is required before any bucket policy can be attached to a bucket
It only affects objects uploaded before 2023
questions.explain: Block Public Access doesn't change the policy or ACL — it sits on top and refuses to honor the public parts of whatever access rules already exist.
